title: Sitharaman Says India-US Trade Talks Have Hit a 'Plateau'
excerpt: The finance minister said further give-and-take would be 'very, very difficult' for both sides — but negotiations continue toward an interim bilateral trade agreement.
body:
• Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said India and the US have reached a "plateau" in bilateral trade deal talks: "Beyond that plateau, giving or taking might be very, very difficult" — though she added both sides would use any remaining room to operate.
  • What it means for you: no tariff relief is imminent. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said last week a deal was "not imminent" after meeting Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal in the US. No deadline or tariff figures were announced — plan for continued duty uncertainty.
  • The sticking point is the imbalance: Sitharaman said the trade balance is "very much in our favor," and Washington wants to narrow what it sees as losses accumulated over the years.
  • Context: talks began in February 2025; a framework for an interim deal was agreed in February, but the US Supreme Court struck down the legal footing of the preferential tariff mechanism Washington had offered; both sides are now working to conclude an interim bilateral trade agreement.

India and the United States have reached a "plateau" in their trade deal talks, Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said on Monday — and giving or taking more beyond it would be "very, very difficult" for both sides. The remarks, at the Munich Leaders Meeting in New Delhi, are the clearest signal yet that the long-running negotiations have hit a wall.

Eighteen months of hard bargaining

The two countries have been negotiating a trade agreement since February 2025, seeking to deepen economic ties and resolve long-standing market-access issues, according to Reuters. In February, they agreed on a framework for an interim trade agreement — but signing never followed after the US Supreme Court struck down the legal footing of the preferential tariff mechanism Washington had offered, forcing both sides back to the table.

The plateau comment follows a week of mixed signals. Prime Minister Narendra Modi spoke to President Donald Trump on September 30, and Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal met US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer in Milwaukee. Goyal called the discussion "productive" in a post on X, saying the two were working toward "early conclusion of a mutually beneficial interim agreement." Greer, for his part, said last week that an agreement was not imminent.

"The agreement negotiations are still ongoing, although we'd like to believe that both the sides have reached a plateau beyond which giving or taking might be very, very difficult. But maybe if there is room to operate from, both sides would do it."

— Nirmala Sitharaman, Finance Minister of India

The imbalance at the heart of it

Sitharaman framed the impasse around the trade balance. "But what is the predominant feature of the trade relations between India and the US? The trade balance is very much in our favor," she said. Washington, she added, would naturally try to narrow the gap and address what it regards as losses accumulated over the years.

She also described a shift in how countries negotiate. "Tariff was an instrument of negotiation, and tariff had a certain framework within which you will apply it. Today framework is there, tariffs are going," she said — while stressing that countries still need to negotiate and find "some give and take."

On a separate friction point — India's Russian oil purchases — Sitharaman said she was aware of no European counterpart to the US "Lindsey Graham bill" that could shape negotiations with the European Union.

"But what is the predominant feature of the trade relations between India and the US? The trade balance is very much in our favor."

— Nirmala Sitharaman, Finance Minister of India

What it means for the diaspora

For NRIs, the implications are practical rather than political. Indian exporters shipping to the United States — and American businesses built on Indian supply chains — get no tariff relief for now, with no deadline and no tariff schedule announced. Investors in Indian export-oriented equities face the same overhang: a deal would have been a clear positive signal for the rupee and for trade-exposed sectors; its absence keeps the policy risk in place. Reuters noted earlier this year that New Delhi has been holding out for better terms — protecting domestic industry, but extending the wait for certainty.

What to watch

The near-term question is whether the "rooms to operate" Sitharaman mentioned actually exist. Watch for the next round of Goyal-Greer engagement and any movement on the interim bilateral trade agreement both sides say they are working toward. The G20 deliberations under the US chairmanship — which Goyal said he discussed with Greer — offer a parallel track where trade friction could either ease or sharpen. For now, the negotiations she described as "hard and very vigorously negotiated" remain exactly that: ongoing, but with neither side ready to move.

nri_angle: No tariff relief is imminent for NRIs with businesses tied to India-US supply chains or investments in trade-exposed sectors — duty uncertainty continues with no deadline announced.
